claims.text: Applying a silicide coating to boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Uncoated boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment suffer aggressive attack by molten aluminum.
Pack cementation can be used to deposit a silicide coating.
Pack cementation can produce a thin silicide coating on a boride-based component.
Approximately 660°C is a typical molten-aluminum plating temperature.
The silicide coating will form an outer high-silicon MSi2 layer and an inner MSi layer.
The dual-layer silicide coating will develop a dense, self-healing oxide film that seals defects and cracks.
During molten-aluminum exposure, the silicide coating will oxidize preferentially and form an adherent protective barrier.
The protective oxide barrier will restrict aluminum penetration and minimize contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
Restricting aluminum penetration and contact with the boride will reduce corrosive attack.
Relative to uncoated boride components, coated components will show markedly lower weight loss.
Relative to uncoated boride components, coated components will show fewer or shallower corrosion pits and reduced corrosion depth.
Relative to uncoated boride components, coated components will retain better overall integrity.
The silicide coating is expected to remain effective under conventional hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Performance under extreme thermal cycling or non-standard chemical exposure has not been established.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement will depend on coating uniformity, coating thickness, and processing parameters.
Long-term stability and optimum coating characteristics require experimental validation.
